posts.title: Which Small Details Do Sellers Forget Until It's Too Late?
posts.excerpt: The last few items on the list are boring, easy, and genuinely painful to fix after the fact.
posts.metaDescription: The details home sellers forget before closing: canceling utilities, earnest money handling, keys and warranties, and final walkthrough preparation.

body.p: Most of selling a home is strategy — price, presentation, negotiation. Then there's a short list of purely administrative items that nobody thinks about until they've become a problem.
None of these will cost you the sale. Several will cost you money, time, or an unpleasant week after you've already moved.

body.h: Cancel the utilities. Put it on the calendar.

body.p: This is the one sellers forget most, and untangling it later is a genuine pain. Put a calendar reminder tied to your closing date and work through the full list:

list: Internet, security monitoring, and anything else on autopay

body.p: Time the cancellations for the day after closing, not before. A house with the water off during a final walkthrough creates problems, and a buyer can't verify that plumbing works without it.

body.h: Never hold the earnest money yourself

body.p: Ask the buyer to send earnest money to the title company, which holds it at no cost and disburses it appropriately at closing. Holding a buyer's deposit personally is a lawsuit waiting to happen, and it gains you nothing whatsoever.

Worth repeating because it keeps happening. A seller who was friendly with his buyers casually said they'd handle the air conditioning "if it happens to go out." The furnace died during the final walkthrough. The buyers refused to sign, and he paid $6,000 to close a sale he'd already moved out for.
Stay friendly and stay slightly formal. Let the buyer raise their own concerns, then make a judgment call once you know what they actually care about.

body.pull: Prorated taxes, HOA dues, and utilities are settled at closing. Your share is real money — know it before you see the settlement statement.

body.h: Gather the paperwork buyers will want

list: Appliance manuals and any transferable warranties
Receipts and permits for major work — roof, HVAC, electrical, windows
Paint colors and any remaining matched paint
HOA documents, rules, and contact information
Every key, garage remote, mailbox key, gate code, and alarm code

body.p: Assembling this in a single folder takes an hour and makes the closing table dramatically less stressful. Missing keys and unrecorded gate codes are a surprisingly common last-minute scramble.

The buyer will walk the home shortly before closing, expecting it broom-clean, empty of everything not included in the sale, and in the condition it was in when they agreed to buy it. Leave nothing behind that wasn't negotiated — including the items in the garage you were hoping they wouldn't mind.

body.h: Then run your net proceeds one more time

body.p: Sale price, minus your loan payoff, minus professional fees, minus prorated expenses, minus any costs you agreed to cover. Knowing that number before you sit down means no unpleasant math at the table.

Catching the small items before they become expensive ones is unglamorous and it's most of what a good advisor actually does. At HomePilot it's part of the flat fee — the checklist work included, not billed by the hour.
Boring, quick, and much easier now than in three weeks.
